beats.text: Every day, you repeat the same little moves on your PC.
Opening the same programs. Arranging the same windows. Hunting for the volume. Clicking through the same menus.
What if a {key}single key could do all of that? Or a {mouse}flick of the mouse? Or simply... {voice}your voice?
This is K-Desktop.

In this video, we'll walk through everything it can do, and how it works under the hood. {commands}Commands, {quickmenus}QuickMenus, {events}events, {macros}macros and {kboard}K-Board. {voice}Voice control, your {phone}phone as a remote, and the new {assistants}assistants that live on top of your windows.
K-Desktop is built around one simple idea: {command}the command.
A command is a {named}named sequence of actions. {open}Open a program, {wait}wait a second, {snap}snap its window to the left, {volume}set the volume to twenty percent. {steps}Step by step, in order.

And a command can be launched from almost anywhere. A {hotkey}hotkey or a {mouse}mouse button. A {quickmenu}QuickMenu, or the {launcher}launcher. Your {voice}voice, your {phone}phone, or the {network}network. {event}Something that happens on your PC. Or even an {assistant}assistant.
Around commands live a few companions. {macros}Macros that replay what you do. {kboard}K-Board profiles that remap your keys. And a {history}history that remembers every run.
It's a {portable}single portable program for {windows}Windows 10 and 11, in {languages}six languages. {local}Everything runs locally, and your {data}data stays in your own folder.
Let's build one. On the Commands page, click {new}New command, and give it a name: {name}Work mode.
Next, a hotkey. Press any combination: {ctrl}Control, {alt}Alt, {w}W.
A hotkey can also be a {mouse}mouse button, like Mouse 5. A {chord}chord of two buttons, like Mouse 4 plus left click. Or the {wheel}wheel with a modifier, like Control plus Wheel Up.
Now, the actions. {run}Run application: Notepad. {wait}Wait one second. {window}Window: left half. {volume}Volume: twenty percent. {folder}Open folder: Documents.
Press {ctrl}Control, {alt}Alt, {w}W... and it {all}all happens, in order, in a fraction of a second.
There are {more}more than thirty actions, grouped into {nine}nine families.
Open and run: {programs}programs, {folders}folders, {special}special Windows locations, {web}web pages in the browser you choose, and {scripts}CMD or PowerShell scripts.
Windows: {max}maximize, place in {halves}halves, {quarters}quarters or {thirds}thirds, {center}center, move to {monitor}another monitor, make {transparent}transparent, or keep {top}on top.
Keyboard and mouse: {keys}send keys or text, {clipboard}transform the clipboard, {macro}play a macro, {kboard}switch a K-Board profile, or {dictate}dictate.
Sound: the {volume}volume of the speakers, the microphone or a single app. {output}Switch the audio output, {play}play sounds, and {record}record audio, even the last few seconds.
Screen: {shot}screenshots, {ocr}copying text straight from the screen, a {magnifier}magnifier, {brightness}brightness and projection, and the {theme}light or dark theme of Windows.
Network: {http}web requests for Home Assistant or any API, {wol}waking another computer with Wake on LAN, and {radio}Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.
System: {hidden}hidden files, the {plan}power plan, and {power}shutting down, restarting or sleeping, with a {countdown}countdown you can cancel.
And flow: {message}show a message, {wait}wait, {menu}open a QuickMenu, {commands}run or switch other commands. The {ninth}ninth family belongs to the assistants. We'll get there.

One flow action deserves a closer look: {if}If. It checks something first. Is a {program}program open? What {time}time is it? Is a {device}device connected? How busy is the {cpu}CPU? When the answer is {no}no, it {stop}stops the command, or {skip}skips the next actions. So one command can take {paths}different paths.

Each command has its own options, too. Limit it to {apps}certain applications: if the same hotkey exists for {every}every app and for {one}one in particular, inside that app, the {wins}specific one wins. {block}Block the key so the app never sees it. Add a {sound}sound, {notes}notes, and extra {phrases}phrases to call it by voice.

K-Desktop runs as {admin}administrator, so its hotkeys work even over {elevated}elevated windows. But {each}each action decides whether its program starts as {asadmin}administrator, or as your {user}normal user.

And every command gets an icon {auto}automatically. Or you pick one: {symbols}any Windows symbol in {colors}fifteen colors, {winicons}Windows icons, your own {images}images, or a {favicon}website's own logo.
Sometimes, one key per command isn't enough. That's what {qm}QuickMenus are for.
Press a hotkey, say {mouse5}Mouse 5, and a menu {blooms}blooms right where your pointer is. Translucent, with {icons}icons, {titles}titles, {separators}separators and {submenus}submenus.

{left}Left click runs a command and closes the menu. {right}Right click runs it and keeps the menu open, perfect for {nudging}nudging the volume. {middle}Middle click jumps straight to editing that item. And the whole menu works from the {keyboard}keyboard, too.

Menus are built in the {editor}editor. {drag}Drag commands from the palette onto the menu: {above}above, {below}below, or {inside}inside an item. {rename}Rename, change icons, {nest}nest submenus, {undo}undo and redo, and choose a {size}size, from compact to huge.
Need something new? A {quick}quick command turns a {program}program, a {folder}folder or a {web}web address into a menu item, in one step.
For everything else, there's the {launcher}launcher: a search box with its own {hotkey}hotkey.
Type a few letters, even loose ones. {c}C, M, F, Y finds {comfy}ComfyUI. It searches your {commands}commands and every program in the {start}Start menu, {store}Store apps included.
Type a {sum}sum, and it's a calculator: {enter}Enter copies the result. And when {nothing}nothing matches, it offers to {web}search the web.
It learns what you use {most}most, and puts it first, before you even {type}type.
So far, you trigger the commands. {events}Events let your PC trigger them for you. {when}When this happens, run these commands.

There are {sixteen}sixteen kinds of triggers. When K-Desktop {start}starts or exits. {time}At a time, or every few {interval}minutes. When a {program}program opens, or comes to the {front}front. After a while {idle}without using the PC. When you {lock}lock it, or it goes to sleep. When a laptop switches to {battery}battery.

When a {controller}controller, a {usb}USB drive, {headphones}headphones or any other device is connected. When you join a {network}network. When a new {file}file appears in a folder. When the {cpu}CPU, the graphics card or the memory crosses a threshold. Or when {remote}another computer, a script or Home Assistant calls it by name.
For example: {when}when Steam opens, {switch}switch the audio output to the headphones.
Many triggers also have a {ends}When it ends side. {closes}When Steam closes, {back}back to the speakers. {nosecond}No second event needed.
Events can have {conditions}conditions, a {cooldown}minimum time between runs, and built-in {loops}protection against loops, so an event can never keep setting itself off.
Some tasks can't be described as actions. You just have to do them. {again}Again, and again. That's what {macros}macros are for.
Press {record}Record, and do the task. K-Desktop captures every {key}key, {click}click, {scroll}scroll and {move}movement, with its exact {timing}timing. {stop}Shift plus Escape finishes.

Every step can be {edited}edited, {dragged}dragged, {inserted}inserted or {deleted}deleted. And {simplify}Simplify cleans it up in one click: {merge}merge presses, {drop}drop mouse movements, {halve}halve the pauses, or {cap}cap them at one second.
Play it from any command: {once}once, {several}several times, in a {loop}loop, or at a different {speed}speed.
And for games, there's {game}game mode. The mouse is recorded as {raw}raw, relative movement: the kind games read, even when they {lock}lock the pointer.
{kboard}K-Board changes what your keys and mouse buttons actually do.
You edit a profile on a {drawn}drawn keyboard and mouse. {click}Click a key, {choose}choose what it becomes, and it {lights}lights up with its new job.
A key can become {key}another key, a {combo}combination, a piece of {text}text, one of your {command}commands, or {nothing}nothing at all.
{caps}Caps Lock as Control. The {win}Windows key disabled while you play. The {side}side buttons as copy and paste.
With {modifiers}modifiers, you get layers: {ctrlj}Control plus J can do something completely different from {j}J.
A profile can work {everywhere}everywhere, or only in {apps}certain apps. And you switch it on and off from a {command}command, or from the {tray}tray icon.
Now, the {voice}voice. K-Desktop understands spoken orders, entirely {local}on your PC, without the {internet}internet.
There are two ways to talk. {hold}Hold the voice hotkey while you speak. Or {tap}tap it once, and just talk: it {stops}stops when you go quiet.
Or use a {wake}wake word. {kd}K-Desktop, open the browser. {nokey}No key at all.

The wake word is yours, and you record it in under a minute. {silence}Three seconds of silence, to measure the background noise. {word}The word itself, several times. And {speech}ten seconds of normal speech, so everyday conversation never sets it off. It can even be a {madeup}made-up word.
So, what happens to every sound? First, {echo}echo cancellation removes whatever your PC is playing, so music or a film won't drown out your voice.

Every {eighty}eighty milliseconds, the {oww}openWakeWord models turn the audio into a compact {fingerprint}fingerprint. Your {personal}personal detector compares it with your own recordings, in {two}two different ways. And {agree}both have to agree.
When it fires, a {second}second check kicks in. {parakeet}Parakeet transcribes the last few seconds, and {confirms}confirms that it really sounds like your word.
{silero}Silero, a voice activity detector, notices when you {stop}stop talking.
And {parakeet}Parakeet, NVIDIA's multilingual speech recognition model, turns your order into {text}text, right there on your PC.
Then comes the clever part: {finding}finding the command you meant.

The first layer reads the {words}words. It looks for a command's {name}name in what you said. It ignores {filler}filler words like please, different word {endings}endings, small {slips}slips, and words that just {sound}sound alike. {youtube}You tube becomes YouTube.

When the words aren't enough, the second layer looks at the {meaning}meaning. {gemma}EmbeddingGemma, a small model from Google, turns sentences into {vectors}vectors: points in a {space}space where similar meanings sit close together.
So, {clean}clean out the trash lands right next to your command, {empty}Empty Recycle Bin. Without a single list of synonyms.

It also knows what isn't yours. {tv}Turn off the TV is close to {shutdown}Shut down the computer, but it's even closer to a list of {everyday}everyday requests that K-Desktop doesn't handle. So {nothing}nothing happens. Anything that {powers}powers off the PC has to be said especially clearly.
You can {chain}chain orders, too. {open}Open YouTube {and}and empty the recycle bin, runs both.
Music and volume work without any command at all. {pause}Pause. {next}Next song. {quieter}A little quieter. {forty}Volume to forty percent. {play}Play music.
And {dictation}dictation types what you say, wherever the cursor is. Say {newline}new line, {scratch}scratch that, or {stopd}stop dictating.

The models are {once}downloaded once. They take about {ram}seven hundred megabytes of memory while loaded, and {free}free it after a while unused. While you speak, {duck}other sounds can be turned down so it hears you better. And {never}neither your audio nor your words ever leave the PC.
Your PC, from the {couch}couch. K-Desktop includes a {webapp}web app for your phone, or any browser.
Pair a device by {scan}scanning a QR code. The code works {once}only once, and any device can be {revoke}revoked at any time.
Your {qm}QuickMenus and {all}all your commands are right there, with {search}search, and your {most}most used ones first.
A {touchpad}touchpad and a {keyboard}keyboard move the PC's mouse, and type for you.
The audio tab controls the {volume}volume, the {music}music, and the {output}output device.
The phone's {mic}microphone gives voice orders. And you can {chat}chat with your assistants.
Install it on the {home}home screen, like an app. Behind a {proxy}reverse proxy with HTTPS, it even works from {outside}outside your home.
There's also an {android}Android app. The same interface, with a {native}native microphone, kept up to date by the {pc}PC itself.

And for machines, there's {udp}UDP, compatible with K-Desktop 4, on port 2501. Send {list}list, to get the remote commands. A {number}number or a name, to run one. {sk}S K plus keys, to press them. Or {event}event plus a name, to fire a Call from outside event. Perfect for {ha}Home Assistant, scripts, or another PC.
And from the {cli}command line: {run}run a command, {menu}open a menu, {fire}fire an event, or {launcher}open the launcher.
Everything that runs ends up in the {history}history. The last {five}five hundred runs: where they {where}came from, how {long}long they took, and whether anything went {wrong}wrong.

As you use K-Desktop, you unlock {ach}achievements. More than a {hundred}hundred of them, each with an {toast}animated notification. {owl}Night owl, for running a command between three and five in the morning. {pianist}Pianist, for a mouse button chord. And a few {secret}secret ones.

And the {stats}statistics count it all. {run}Commands and actions run, {menus}QuickMenus opened, {voice}voice orders, how many were understood by their {meaning}meaning, and {sources}where your commands come from.
{settings}Settings are grouped by topic, and {search}searchable with Control F.
{appearance}Appearance: {theme}light, dark, or follow Windows. {languages}Six built-in languages, and you can add your {own}own with a JSON file.
{general}General: start with {windows}Windows, with administrator rights and no prompt. {hotkeys}Hotkeys to show, exit or pause K-Desktop. {sounds}Sounds, and on-screen {osd}messages.
{disable}Disable in: a list of apps, like your {games}games, where hotkeys do nothing, unless a command is set to {always}always run.
The {launcher}launcher, {voice}voice, {multimedia}multimedia, {captures}captures and magnifier, the {web}web app and {remote}remote control: each has its own section.

And your data is safe. {daily}Automatic daily backups. {zip}Full zip copies every few days. {export}Export and import. And a one-click {import}import from K-Desktop 4. {updates}Updates install themselves.
And finally, something new: {assistants}assistants. Little characters that live on top of your {windows}windows. You can {talk}talk to them, and they can actually {do}do things.

Meet the {lander}Lander, a tiny lunar module that flies around and lands on your title bars, with a {game}game of its own. {kobii}Kobii, a squishy creature that wanders along your taskbar. And {pip}Pip, a drop made with nothing but {json}images and JSON.
Assistants live in an {optional}optional module. While it's {off}off, K-Desktop doesn't load any of it.

Each assistant is a {package}package. Open one, and its {card}card tells you what it is, whether its {signature}signature checks out, and {what}what it can do. {installs}Install it, and it drops right onto your desktop.

Assistants run in their {process}own process, without {admin}administrator rights, and talk to K-Desktop through a {pipe}private, locked down pipe. K-Desktop draws them on a {layer}transparent layer on your graphics card, and your windows become their {terrain}terrain.

To talk to one, say its {name}name. {question}Lander, what time is it? Each assistant can have its {own}own wake word, while {kd}K-Desktop keeps running your commands. You can also {key}hold its key, or {click}hold the click on the character itself. And when it {asks}asks you something back, just answer.

Their {brain}brain is a language model, and it runs {pc}on your PC. With {llama}llama server and a model downloaded from {hf}Hugging Face, it picks the {biggest}biggest one that fits your graphics card. It also works with {ollama}Ollama, or any {openai}OpenAI compatible server. And it always tells you {where}where your words go: {thispc}this PC, {network}your network, or the {internet}internet.

The model {loads}loads when you talk, {unloads}unloads when idle, and {games}gets out of the way when a game goes full screen. Simple things, like the {time}time, a {timer}timer, a {note}note or {cancel}cancel, are answered instantly by {rules}fixed rules, without the AI.

And they {aloud}answer out loud, {sentence}sentence by sentence, while the AI is still writing. With {kokoro}Kokoro, a natural voice that runs offline on your processor. The same voice you're {hearing}hearing right now. Or {piper}Piper, with voices in every language. Or the {windows}Windows voices. Or just {beeps}beeps.

Each assistant brings its own {style}style. The Lander talks over the {radio}mission control radio. You can {mix}mix two voices, try {robot}robot, martian or eight bit, keep them {quiet}quiet during a full screen film, and even hear them from the {side}side of the screen where they are.

What can they do? A lot. {timers}Timers, {notes}notes, {calc}calculations, the {weather}weather. {web}Searching and reading the web. {files}Finding files, {apps}opening apps, {music}controlling the music, {pc}checking the PC, {screen}looking at your screen, and running your own {commands}commands.
To keep a small model sharp, only the {three}three to five tools that fit each order reach it, chosen by their {examples}example phrases and by {meaning}meaning.
Anything {risky}risky asks first. Say {yes}yes once, or {always}yes and don't ask again. And many actions can be {undo}undone.

And you see it happen. Ask: {ask}Lander, minimize Chrome. It {flies}flies over, {fires}fires at the button, and the window {impact}minimizes right on impact. To move a window, it shoots a {hook}grappling hook at the title bar, and {tows}tows it into place.

You can also give them new skills without compiling anything: one {json}JSON file per tool. Call any {api}web API, like Home Assistant. Run one of your {command}commands with your own phrases. Chain a {routine}routine. Or run your own {script}script. {secrets}Secrets like tokens are stored encrypted, and the model {never}never sees them. And {mcp}MCP servers plug their tools in too, imported straight from {claude}Claude Desktop.
They {remember}remember what matters: your name, what you like, important dates. You can {see}see and edit everything they know about you, and keep {notes}notes.

And they can {read}read your documents. Choose {folders}folders or files: notes, manuals, contracts, PDFs, Word, even {scanned}scanned pages, with the text recognition of Windows. Everything is {once}read once, on your PC, and kept up to date. Ask: {ask}what does my contract say about the deposit? And they {answer}answer, telling you which {source}document and page it came from.

Assistants plug into commands, too. Four {four}actions let any command or event run an assistant's {action}action, {ask}ask it something, make it {say}say something, or {free}free its brain before a game.
And if you want to build your own, there's an {sdk}SDK with a template. Or {nocode}no code at all: just images and JSON, like {pip}Pip.
{commands}Commands and actions. {qm}QuickMenus and the launcher. {events}Events, macros and K-Board. Your {voice}voice, your {phone}phone, and {assistants}assistants that lend a hand.
K-Desktop is a {single}single portable program for Windows. {download}Download it from GitHub, and start with {one}one command. You'll be surprised how {far}far it goes.
Thanks for watching.
